blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this SOUPS 2019 paper as a well-structured study on the prevalence and characteristics of ransomware victims in the U.S. The paper stands out for its rigorous survey methodology, including a representative sample of 1,180 U.S. adults and careful validation of self-reported ransomware incidents. The key findings include an estimated 2-3% annual victimization rate (translating to millions of infections per year) and a surprisingly low ransom payment rate of just 4%. The paper also develops a risk assessment model identifying six factors that predict ransomware vulnerability, such as lack of two-factor authentication, poor backup habits, and prior exposure to online scams. Colyer notes the study's practical value in quantifying the ransomware threat and informing user education efforts.

Consumers are thought to be the most common victims of ransomware [5, 7]. While most attacks are thought to be untargeted, consumers are often less likely to have robust security in place, increasing the likelihood of falling victim to an attack [7]. Despite the harm ransomware can inflict, relatively little is known about the prevalence and characteristics of such attacks in the general population. Reliable estimates of the prevalence of ransomware are necessary both for understanding the nature of today’s threat landscape, as well as for longer-term comparison and analysis. Various government, industry organizations, and researchers have attempted to document the phenomenon, but results have been often inconsistent. This is in large part due to the non-representative data they are based on. Industry reports are typically published by security firms and are based on users of their software products. Such samples are thus inevitably biased towards a set of consumers who have sufficient security awareness and the financial resources to purchase such products. Their experiences may thus not reflect those of the general population. In contrast, government agencies typically report rates based on voluntary victim reports. These estimates are thought to grossly underestimate the true rate [33]. For example, the U.S. Department of Justice estimates that only 15 percent of the nation’s fraud victims report their crimes to law enforcement [2], however it is unclear what the true rate of reporting is in the general population.
